newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria energy sector to fight hyperinflation.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria energy sector to fight hyperinflation.

text.p: Bulgaria's energy sector, hamstrung by the headlong fall of the lev, plans emergency measures to survive amid the country's deepening economic crisis and political unrest, energy officials said on Monday.

Economists said last week Bulgaria's economy had plunged into hyper-inflation for the first time. The monthly inflation rate for January was expected to hit 50 percent after inflation for the first 15 days of the month ran to 30.8 percent.

"We were prepared to work under a currency board (this year) and now we need emergency measures for operating under the conditions of a hyper-inflation," Deputy Energy Minister Ivanka Dilovska told a news conference.

The ministry has submitted proposals to the outgoing cabinet designed to change some of the parametres of the current mechanism, which revises energy prices each month mainly according to inflation and the lev/dollar exchange rate.

"We have proposed to change the pricing scheme as it was designed to work in a stable macro-economic situation while now it cannot keep up the required price of 3.5 cents per kilowatt hour," Dilovska said. "Things are the same with coal."

Changes are aimed at easing the delayed impact of the pricing scheme as the January prices have been based on the lev/dollar rate in the first 15 days of December -- 405 levs. Under the scheme prices should be raise by 35 percent from February 1 based on 580 levs per dollar, Dilovska said.
The energy ministry also aims to increase heating prices, which the cabinet had frozen since last October when they were $14.4 per gigacalory.

"Now it is only 3.5 cents while we envisaged $20 per gigacalory in the stabilising programme," Dilovska said, adding that 1997 should be the first year in the implementation of a stabilising programme in the debt-ridden energy sector.
The lev hit new lows around 950 to the dollar on the interbank market on Monday from 600 at the beginning of January.
As a result the sale price of electricity has dropped to an average of 1.5 cents per kilowatt hour while it has hit its peak of 3.6 cents last October.
The ministry has started selling some of its assets to extend credits to the nearly bankrupt heating plants to buy oil fuel and thus ensure their operation during the winter, Dilovska said.
The International Monetary Fund proposed last year the implementation of a currency board to halt the freefall of the lev.
A political deadlock created by ruling Socialists' refusal to accept opposition calls for early parliamentary elections has postponed talks with the IMF on strict monetary measures.

The opposition says that if early elections were held in March, the new parliament would adopt the legal amendments needed for the implementation of a currency board in April and enable its introduction in May.

The energy sector, which imports 86 percent of its resources, needs a greater hard currency profit which it hopes to gain from exporting electricity when free capacity is available and through awarding concessions to existing gas pipelines transiting Russian natural gas to the Balkans.
Bulgaria exports 300-400 megawatts of electricity to Turkey and hopes to double that in the near future, officials said, adding that monthly income from these exports was some $10 million.
